name: lastz
why: A real DNA pairwise aligner you can run on genomes at home, a legitimate bioinformatics rabbit hole.

brief.what_it_is: LASTZ is a command-line pairwise aligner for DNA sequences, written in C. You give it a target sequence file and a query sequence file (FASTA, Nib, or 2Bit, with optional FASTQ and other inputs), and it writes alignments to stdout in formats such as MAF, LAV, AXT, SAM, PAF, BLASTN-style, or a general tab-delimited format. It can also infer scoring parameters from the sequences. It is a drop-in replacement for BLASTZ and accepts BLASTZ's command-line syntax, plus many extra options.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a more capable, backward-compatible successor to BLASTZ, offering extra options and different results from BLASTZ for DNA-to-DNA alignment of whole chromosomes, short reads, and self-alignments. The author is Bob Harris of the Miller Lab at Penn State.
brief.how_it_works: LASTZ runs a staged pipeline. It indexes the target's seed words in a position table, then for each query finds seeds (short near-matches), extends them gap-free into HSPs, chains HSPs into syntenic anchors, extends those with gapped alignment, filters by score and user criteria, and interpolates in the gaps at higher sensitivity. The query's reverse complement is processed as well. Sensitivity is tuned with options such as --step, --seed, --notransition, --nogapped, and --chain.

brief.install_notes: Download the source from github.com/lastz/lastz or the Miller Lab archive. Unpack, cd into the src directory, then run make and make install. Set the LASTZ_INSTALL shell variable or edit make-include.mak to choose the install directory, and add that directory to your PATH. Needs a C compiler, with gcc named as the reference; other compilers can be used by editing the Makefile. Some ancillary tools are Python but use only standard-library modules. Solaris users should use gmake. No accounts or GPUs are required. Optional build variants include lastz_32 for genomes over 2 Gb and an experimental lastz_40 for genomes over 4 Gb; any build can enable adjacent indels.
brief.standout: It is a drop-in BLASTZ replacement with a very deep option set, including coverage and identity filters, dynamic target masking, interpolation of alignments at higher sensitivity, and explicit control over HSP and chaining stages. Its docs also lay out a worked example that aligns reads to a chromosome using the same tool.
brief.status: maintained. The GitHub README says it was updated Sep/28/2026 by Bob Harris and that 1.04.60 is the latest official release. The homepage says the release was built September 28, 2026. The repo describes its branch as the latest official working branch. Note the homepage intro says 'Date: August 2021', so the docs' own dates are inconsistent. I did not check commit history or the releases page.
brief.caveats: The author says the working branch may be less stable than tagged releases. Legacy releases before September 2021 are no longer on the Miller Lab site, which the docs say is only 1.04.15 and earlier. Some options need special builds: inference is described as experimental and requires a special build. The 2 Gb and 4 Gb limits need the lastz_32 and lastz_40 builds. Adjacent indels are off by default and need a build flag. Full-genome runs are slow: the human-vs-chicken chromosome example takes 4.5 hours at default settings. The build treats warnings as errors, so a clean build may need Makefile.warnings. Platform is Unix-like; the author developed it on macOS. Shotgun-read examples depend on test data shipped in the distribution. The docs' own date and version statements are inconsistent, and I could not confirm the license from the pages I read.
quotes: LASTZ is a drop-in replacement for BLASTZ, and is backward compatible with BLASTZ's command-line syntax.
LASTZ: A tool for (1) aligning two DNA sequences, and (2) inferring appropriate scoring parameters automatically.
Users are encouraged to use a tagged release, as this working branch may not be stable.
